newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 12.

text.p: A warning by Reserve Bank governor Don Brash that next year's tax cuts might have to be deferred if government spending increased was largely accepted by coalition negotiators on Monday night. Tight control of spending was one of the few measures that would help lower New Zealand's relatively high interest and exchange rates, Brash told a Federated Farmers meeting in Invercargill. NZ First leader Winston Peters gave the speech a "cautious welcome". Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen accepted the need for caution in spending, but noted all three prospective coalition parties were budgeting for surpluses. Page 1.
The Labour Party and the Alliance have backed the Government's call for the United Nations to intervene in the Zairean crisis. Page 1.

The annual cost of child abuse was $1.5 billion, which could be reduced if the Government put sufficient funds into preventive measures, Labour social welfare spokewoman Annette King said on Monday. She gave out copies of a Social Welfare draft report, which covered an estimated 26,820 abuse cases,
saying it proved the Government was "wilfully underfunding" the Children, Young Persons and Their Families Service. Page 2.
Agriculture Minister Lockwood Smith left on Monday for the World Food Summit in Rome, where he will spread the word against non-tariff barriers in international food trade. Page 2.

Supermarkets and grocers want to be able to sell spirits and beers as well as wine, the Retail and Wholesale Merchants Association say in a submission to the Sale of Liquor Act review. And they want to sell them every day, including Sundays.

A Reserve Bank-sponsored academic has suggested the central bank take control of raising and lowering income tax rates to fight inflation. The suggestion comes from United States economist Laurence Ball, a professorial fellow in monetary economics at Wellington's Victoria University. The position is supported by the Reserve Bank. Page 15.

A cashed-up Brierley Investments was well-placed for new investments, BIL chief executive Paul Collins said in Sydney on Monday. Collins said the sell-down of BIL's stake in British hotel group Thistle had resulted in a further strengthening pf the company's already-strong position. BIL now had equity of $4.1 billion and total assets of $7.3 billion, including $1.2 billion in cash. Page 15.

Strong government surpluses and steadily reducing debt will feature under either a Labour or National government, according to London-based economic analysts UBS. The Union Bank of Switzerland said political uncertainty had "diminished considerably" since the election, though no one knew which party would form the government. Page 15.

Progressive Enterprises is making no provision for $1.14 million worth of claims made against it by former employees. The supermarket operator's annual report says the directors believe the claims are "quite without merit", but gives no details on how many claims have been made, or on what basis. Page 15.

The New Zealand Oil and Gas management is set to come under fire at its annual meeting this month from a consortium which has built a 10 percent stake. The impetus behind the move is the consortium's belief that the company is not trying to maximise shareholder wealth. If enough support can be gained, a push might be made to replace the management. This could spur a breaking up of the company. Several of the consortium members are believed to be working alongside parties in Australia in examining the assets of NZOG. The first six months of the financial year would be fairly flat for Ports of Auckland but longer term prospects were bright, said chairman Sir Richard Carter on Monday.

Exchangeable shares in Independent Press Communications made a quiet debut on the stock exchange on Monday at 830 cents, well below a value of 904 cents put on them by an Irish broker, Davy Equity Research. A parcel of the shares was traded off market before the start of trade at 830 cents and a further 1,000 later
changed hands at the closing price of 820 cents.
